title: G7 Trade War Erupts Over Digital Tax, BOJ Hikes to 31-Year High, Hormuz Mine Clearing to Take 50 Days
subhead: Trump threatens 100% tariffs on French wine at G7 while the Bank of Japan raises rates to their highest since 1995 and oil markets price in a slow Hormuz reopening despite the US-Iran ceasefire deal.

sections.heading: G7 Spirals Into Transatlantic Trade War Over Digital Tax
sections.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron refused to scrap France's 3% digital services tax on US tech giants at the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, prompting President Trump to threaten 100% tariffs on French wine. Macron shot back: 'The US does not decide European law.' The clash threatens to overshadow the summit's focus on the Iran deal and Ukraine.

The dispute is not merely rhetorical. France's digital services tax, which targets revenue generated by large tech companies operating in France regardless of where they are headquartered, has been a long-running sore point for Washington. Trump's threat of a blanket 100% wine tariff — a category worth roughly $2 billion in annual French exports to the US — would be among the most punitive trade actions between Western allies in decades.

At the same summit, Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi pushed a coordinated G7 response to China's trade tactics, while Canadian PM Mark Carney raised China EV tariffs with Trump. Japan also proposed a joint critical minerals stockpiling initiative to counter China's dominance in rare earth supply chains, and the Trump administration floated a plan for a Western critical minerals pricing bloc — though both proposals faced skepticism from allies. (BBC, Nikkei Asia, headlines)
sections.whyItMatters: A 100% wine tariff would be an extraordinary escalation between NATO allies and signals that Trump is willing to weaponize trade against partners as readily as adversaries. The digital tax fight could fracture G7 unity precisely when coordinated action on Iran, Ukraine, and China is most needed.

sections.heading: Bank of Japan Raises Rates to 31-Year High, Signals More Ahead
sections.body:
The Bank of Japan raised its key policy rate to its highest level in 31 years, marking a landmark step in Japan's monetary policy normalization. The BOJ also signaled readiness to tighten further as it focuses on taming price pressures driven by the Iran-war-induced energy shock, according to headline reports.

Nikkei Asia reports that early rate-rise bets have increased as the yen reached a multidecade low, with US-Iran tensions fueling oil price surges and inflation worries. Markets are now pricing in a more aggressive BOJ trajectory. The Nikkei 225 rose 152 points (0.24%) to 64,764 in morning trading on July 27, with falling oil prices providing some support, though Kioxia Holdings fell as much as 10% ahead of earnings.

Nikkei sources had previously reported the BOJ was expected to keep rates unchanged at next week's policy meeting, making the hike a surprise. The move reflects growing pressure on the central bank to avoid falling behind the curve on inflation, especially with oil above $100/barrel. (Nikkei Asia, headlines)
sections.whyItMatters: A BOJ rate hike to a 31-year high marks a decisive shift in the world's fourth-largest economy. With the yen at multidecade lows and oil above $100, Japan is choosing to fight imported inflation rather than support growth — a decision that will ripple through global carry trades and capital flows.

sections.heading: Hormuz Demining Could Take 40-50 Days, Oil Premiums Fall but Floor Remains
sections.body:
Demining operations in the Strait of Hormuz involving conventional minesweepers and underwater drones may take 40-50 days before insurers and shipping companies feel confident enough to resume normal traffic, according to headline reports. The timeline means the critical waterway — through which roughly 20 million barrels per day passed before the war — will remain constrained well into September even under the US-Iran ceasefire framework.

At the G7, Trump insisted the Strait of Hormuz would reopen toll-free under the Iran deal and said the US would not need 'much help' in clearing it. But the reality on the water is more cautious: S&P Global data shows just 10 vessels transited the strait on Tuesday, down from 120-140 per day before the war.

Oil spot premiums in Asia have dropped back to pre-war levels following the tentative ceasefire deal, but uncertainty about the pace of Hormuz reopening is keeping a floor under prices. Marine war-risk insurance costs in Hormuz remain at 7.5-10% of hull value, up from 1-3% before the conflict, with total insurance cost for a single tanker transit estimated at roughly $21 million. Trump said at the G7 that oil prices fell 5% to a three-month low on hopes of restored shipping. OPEC separately cut its 2026 oil demand growth forecast for the second time, citing economic uncertainty and the Middle East conflict. (S&P Global via Al Jazeera, headlines)
sections.whyItMatters: A 40-50 day demining timeline means Hormuz disruption will persist through Q3, keeping insurance costs elevated and constraining global oil supply. The gap between Trump's confident G7 rhetoric and operational reality on the water underscores how far the market remains from normalization.

sections.heading: Fed Chair Warsh Faces Hawkish Shift as First Meeting Loomoms
sections.body:
New Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is convening his first FOMC meeting with rate hike expectations rising and the dot plot expected to show a hawkish shift, according to headline reports. Warsh, who replaced Jerome Powell just weeks ago, takes the helm as oil above $100/barrel and the Iran conflict keep inflation pressures elevated.

The ECB is also holding firm. ECB chief economist Philip Lane said the central bank will remain proactive in fighting high inflation despite falling energy prices following the US-Iran deal, signaling rates may stay elevated. Lane's comments suggest the ECB will not be cutting rates soon even if oil cools. (headlines)
sections.whyItMatters: Warsh's first meeting will set the tone for his entire chairmanship. A hawkish dot plot alongside the BOJ's rate hike signals that major central banks are converging on tighter policy despite geopolitical uncertainty — a combination that tightens global financial conditions.

sections.heading: China Cracks Down on Former Top Regulator and Trip.com, Delists Blacklist Decision
sections.body:
China's anti-corruption body announced an investigation into Fang Xinghai, former vice-chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), for 'serious legal and disciplinary violations' — a euphemism for corruption and abuse of power. Fang, 62, who held the regulatory position from October 2015 to July 2024 and holds a doctorate in economics from Stanford, is the latest in a string of senior financial cadres targeted. His former colleague Yi Huiman, CSRC chairman from 2019 to 2024, was found to have used his position for bribes and abuse of power, according to CCDI findings in April.

Separately, China hit Trip.com with $765 million in penalties for monopoly abuse, with the regulator saying the online travel giant forced hotels into exclusive deals and lowest-rate pledges, according to Nikkei Asia.

On the trade front, the Trump administration has delayed adding DeepSeek, CXMT, and over 100 Chinese companies to the trade blacklist, seeking to avoid further escalation with Beijing amid fragile diplomatic ties. The delay marks a tactical pause rather than a policy shift — the administration cited concerns about 'escalation with Beijing' in its decision. (SCMP, Nikkei Asia, headlines)
sections.whyItMatters: The Fang investigation continues Beijing's pattern of targeting senior financial regulators, sending a chill through China's markets just as state agencies launch coordinated stock purchases to arrest declines. The Trip.com penalty and blacklist pause show Beijing simultaneously tightening domestic tech regulation while Washington temporarily eases external pressure.

sections.heading: G7 Allies Ramp Up Russia Sanctions as Zelenskyy Pushes Peace
sections.body:
G7 leaders scrambled to refocus attention on Ukraine at the Evian summit, with Zelenskyy joining a 75-minute working session. The UK announced new sanctions targeting Russia's shadow oil fleet and finance networks, and British troops seized a Russian shadow fleet vessel in the English Channel for the first time. Canada unveiled a package targeting 162 individuals, entities, and vessels linked to Russia's shadow fleet and energy sector.

Trump indicated he may reimpose sanctions on Russian oil soon and told reporters that Russia should make a deal, suggesting Ukraine was 'moving back up' his priority list. But he also downplayed the Ukraine war's significance for the US, revealing persistent transatlantic divisions. Zelenskyy offered to meet Putin face-to-face at the G7 or in the US; Putin has not responded. (headlines)
sections.whyItMatters: The coordinated UK-Canada shadow fleet sanctions and first-ever seizure of a Russian vessel in the English Channel represent a tangible escalation in economic warfare against Moscow. Whether Trump follows through on Russian oil sanctions remains the key variable for global energy markets.

sections.heading: Central Banks Accelerate Gold Buying as De-Dollarization Deepens
sections.body:
Nearly 90% of central banks plan to increase gold holdings as countries diversify reserves away from the US dollar, according to a World Gold Council report cited in headlines. The trend reflects a structural shift in global finance amid geopolitical fragmentation, with gold holding gains as markets assessed the implications of the US-Iran interim peace deal.

Meanwhile, South Korea and Indonesia are tightening oversight of speculative currency derivatives trades as the Iran war-driven oil disruption rattles forex markets in energy-importing economies. The moves reflect growing concern about capital outflows and currency instability in emerging markets facing a terms-of-trade shock from elevated oil prices. (headlines, World Gold Council)
sections.whyItMatters: Near-universal central bank appetite for gold signals that de-dollarization has moved from rhetoric to reserve allocation. Combined with EM currency defense measures, the trend suggests the financial architecture underpinning US dollar dominance is eroding in practice, not just in principle.

bottomLine: A G7 summit meant to showcase Western unity instead exposed its fractures — Trump threatening 100% wine tariffs on France over a digital tax, while allies push sanctions on Russia and debate China trade tactics. The Bank of Japan's surprise rate hike to a 31-year high and Warsh's hawkish turn at the Fed mean the world's two largest central banks are tightening into uncertainty. Oil may have retreated from $100 on Iran ceasefire hopes, but with Hormuz demining taking 40-50 days and insurance costs still at 4x pre-war levels, supply constraints persist. The gold rush by central banks and EM currency defense measures signal that the geopolitical shock is reshaping the plumbing of global finance, not just its politics.
sources: BBC, Nikkei Asia, SCMP, Al Jazeera, S&P Global, World Gold Council, headlines aggregation
